newsitem.title: USA: Coastal allays one PDVSA fear in $1.7-bln oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Coastal allays one PDVSA fear in $1.7-bln oil deal.

text.p: Coastal Corp has allayed a Venezuelan fear that a proposed $1.7 billion upgrading joint venture would displace the U.S. company's current purchases of Venezuelan crude, sources at PDVSA unit Maraven said on Thursday.

Under the proposal, Coastal has agreed to shift its current purchases of 40,000-45,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude for its refinery in Corpus Christi, Texas to the company's 17,500 bpd asphalt refinery in Mobile Bay, Alabama and its 205,000 bpd plant on the Caribbean island of Aruba.
Another PDVSA concern that Coastal would seek to upgrade the crude outside Venezuela, thereby risking the project's preferential income tax treatment, seems to be up in the air.
A top Maraven official said Coastal, like other companies involved in similar upgrading ventures, has agreed to convert the crude at the Venezuelan industrial city of Jose.
But a Coastal spokesman in Houston said the issue is still on the negotiating table. "It's not definite yet," he said. "Those details are still under negotiation."
Under Venezuelan tax law, these ventures are subject to a 34 percent income tax, instead of the normal 66.7 percent, if the Orinoco crude is upgraded within Venezuela.
The project is now pending approval by PDVSA's board of directors. "We did our analysis, submitted it to PDVSA and are awaiting an answer," a Maraven source said.
If PDVSA signs off on the project, it would be submitted to the Venezuelan congress for final approval.
The joint venture company would then invest some $200 million to upgrade the Corpus Christi plant to enable it to process the syncrude, sources said.
The Coastal-Maraven venture is the sixth in a string of proposed upgrading deals between PDVSA and major oil companies.
The projects marry PDVSA's efforts to secure more supply outlets for its sour crude in the key U.S. market with development of its vast extra-heavy crude reserves.
The Orinoco Tar Belt contains an estimated 270 billion barrels of recoverable extra-heavy crude reserves.
